lesson.title: When the model is wrong
lesson.subtitle: Missing rules, shaky numbers, and assumptions in the open

video.title: When the model is wrong
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor Eze — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor in the school kitchen holding a printout; two cooks laughing behind him.
scenes.animation: The printout zooms in on ‘41 coins’; the cooks’ laughter bubbles pop.
scenes.narration: Our new lunch model found the cheapest plate that meets every need: forty-one coins. The cooks laughed. Two handfuls of groundnuts and half a cup of greens, every day, for every child?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: when the model is wrong, and how to find out before the children do.

scenes.visual: A rulebook with only three pages; around it, sticky notes the model never read: variety, taste, allergies, cooking time.
scenes.animation: Sticky notes flutter in around the closed book.
scenes.narration: A model obeys only the rules it is given. Nobody told this one about variety, taste, allergies or how long rice takes to cook. So it did exactly what it was asked, and the answer is still wrong.

scenes.visual: Okafor shows the plate plan to cooks, two pupils and a parent; each adds a sticky note.
scenes.animation: Notes appear one by one and slide into a ‘rules’ box.
scenes.on_screen_text: Ask the people who live with it
scenes.narration: Find the missing rules by showing the answer to the people who live with it. The cooks, the pupils, a parent with an allergic child: each spots something the model can’t. Each objection becomes a new limit or a new goal.

scenes.visual: Two plates side by side: before (41 coins, two handfuls of nuts) and after the rule (43 coins, a spoon of beans circled).
scenes.animation: The new plate fills; the spoon of beans gets a question mark.
scenes.narration: The cooks say: no more than one handful of groundnuts. Solve again, and lunch costs about forty-three coins, two more than before. And look: the model now serves a spoonful of beans, because nobody said portions come in halves.

scenes.visual: A market price board with a price changing, a flooded road sign, an empty teacher’s chair.
scenes.animation: Each picture slides in; a dial labelled ‘change it’ turns.
scenes.narration: Models can also be wrong because their numbers are. A price goes up at the market, a road floods, a teacher leaves. Before you trust a plan, change the numbers you are least sure of, and see whether the plan changes a lot.

scenes.visual: Two before-and-after cards: the map with the flooded bridge, the garden with more tomato beds.
scenes.animation: Each card flips from before to after.
scenes.narration: Flood one bridge, and the shortest way to school goes from thirteen kilometres to fourteen, by a new route. Raise the price of tomatoes, and the best garden plan jumps from three tomato beds to six. A plan that jumps when one number moves needs a second look.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma points at the plan: rice, groundnuts, greens. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! The model’s cheapest lunch has no beans and no eggs at all. What’s the most likely reason?

scenes.visual: The answer card gets a check; a gap in the rulebook glows.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops; the gap highlights.
scenes.on_screen_text: A missing rule, not wrong sums
scenes.narration: The model has no rule about variety, so it skips them. The solver did its job; the model left something out. Mistakes in models are usually missing rules, not wrong sums.

scenes.visual: A one-page assumptions sheet pinned beside the lunch plan.
scenes.animation: Lines write themselves on the sheet.
scenes.narration: So write the model’s assumptions down, in plain words, beside the answer. Which needs it meets, which prices it used and when, and what it ignores. Then anyone, a cook or a parent, can check it and say what’s missing.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: food buttons, nutrient bars, the cheapest plate in a box.
scenes.animation: A finger slides ‘Most portions of one food’ to 4; the plate fills with groundnuts.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: School lunch for less
scenes.narration: In the app, find the cheapest lunch, then allow up to four portions of a food. The cheapest plate becomes almost all groundnuts. Then take foods out of the market, and see what happens.

scenes.visual: Okafor between a group of pupils and the cooks. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The pupils say the cheapest plan is fine, but the cooks say it can’t be cooked in time for lunch. Who is right about the model?

scenes.visual: Four summary lines and a takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: The cooks: cooking time is a missing limit, so the plan can’t really happen. Remember: a model obeys only its rules, so test answers with the people who live with them. Change the shaky numbers and see whether the plan jumps. And write the assumptions beside the answer.

scenes.visual: Pupils raising hands; the board fills with new rules under ‘The model forgot…’.
scenes.animation: Rules are added one by one.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: show pupils a plan a computer could make, such as the cheapest lunch, and ask them to break it. Every objection becomes a rule on the board. Then ask: which rules did the first model miss, and who would have noticed?

checkpoints.prompt: The cheapest lunch has no beans and no eggs at all. What’s the most likely reason?

options.text: The model has no rule about variety, so it skips them

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the solver found the cheapest mix of the rules it was given. Variety was never one of them.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the solver followed its rules exactly. Nothing in the model asks for variety, so cheaper foods win.

checkpoints.prompt: Pupils say the cheapest plan is fine; the cooks say it can’t be cooked in time. Who is right about the model?

options.text: The cooks: cooking time is a missing limit

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a plan that can’t be cooked in time isn’t feasible in real life. Cooking time is a limit the model is missing.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — optimal for the model isn’t possible in the kitchen. The cooks found a missing limit: cooking time.
